summary: Teach the coordinate pair as an ORDERED address read off two perpendicular number lines (x-axis horizontal, y-axis vertical) that meet at the origin (0,0). The first number is distance ALONG the x-axis, the second is distance UP the y-axis, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. Target the two dominant errors: reversal (writing/reading y before x) and counting squares from a grid edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin. Core activities use a plotting/journey task where swapping the same two numbers lands on different points; alternatives include a labelled reference grid and a navigator-talk task that each serve a narrower purpose.
misconceptions: Reversal — gives/reads the pair as (y, x): up before across (NCETM: 'putting the y-coordinate before the x')
Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point
Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
Loses the origin as the (0,0) start, or thinks the axes are just the borders of the grid rather than number lines

activities.title: Along then up: the swapped-pair journey
steps: On a numbered coordinate grid (first quadrant), first point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin. Then start at the origin (0,0) and plot (4,2): move 4 ALONG the x-axis first, then 2 UP, tracing the corridor-then-stairs path and marking the point where the lines cross.
Now plot (2,4) from the origin the same way (2 along, then 4 up) and mark that point too.
Compare: describe out loud where each marker landed and why the two points are in different places on the grid even though they use the same two numbers.
Write a sentence: 'The order matters because ___.'
Check your work: point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin again, and confirm that both journeys started at the origin (0,0).
activities.insight: The pair is an ordered address, not just two numbers: swapping the order sends you to a different place, and every reading starts from the origin and is read off the numbered lines.

activities.title: Read it back: name the pair for a given point
steps: Look at a point shown on a numbered grid and state its coordinate pair, saying the across reading first then the up reading.
For a point such as the one at 3 across and 5 up, write (3,5) and complete: '(3,5) means 3 along the ___-axis and 5 up the ___-axis.'
Decide for a 'same or different' pair such as (2,4) and (4,2) and justify your choice.
Point to the origin and state its coordinates, explaining why it is (0,0).
activities.insight: Reading a point back into an ordered pair uses the same across-then-up convention and the origin as the zero start; naming the axes and origin secures the vocabulary.

activities.title: Labelled grid reference (scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled grid where tapping or pointing to the origin reveals '(0,0), where the axes cross' and a point reveals 'along 3, up 5'.
Use it as a reference to check your own readings after plotting.
Name the x-axis, y-axis and origin from the labels.
activities.insight: A clearly labelled grid consolidates the vocabulary (x-axis, y-axis, origin) and the along-then-up reading as a reference.

activities.title: Navigator talk: give the pair before I move (alternative)
steps: Direct a navigator to a target point you have been shown by giving its coordinate pair, saying the across move first; the navigator moves exactly as told (first number across, second number up), so check whether it reaches the target.
When the navigator asks 'across or up first?', answer and explain before it moves.
Re-state a pair correctly if the navigator queries the order.
activities.insight: Because the navigator always moves the first number across and the second number up, a reversed pair sends it to a different point than the target, which is intended to make the reversal error audible and visible and to prompt self-correction.

checkQuestion: On a coordinate grid, mark point A at (2,4). Ask: 'What are the coordinates of A?' Then plot a second point B at (4,2) and ask: 'And what about B? Are A and B the same point or different — and how do you know? What does each number in the pair tell you?'
checkAnswer: A is (2,4) and B is (4,2) — they are DIFFERENT points. In each pair the first number is the distance ALONG the x-axis (horizontal) from the origin and the second is the distance UP the y-axis (vertical); because the order is swapped, A is 2 across and 4 up while B is 4 across and 2 up, so they land in different places.
